keyVerseText: And the Avites made Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burnt their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim.
rootMeaning: The root of אֲדְרַמֶּלֶךְ (ʼĂdrammelek) combines אָדַר (ʼâdar), meaning to be glorious or honorable, with מֶלֶךְ (melek), meaning king. Thus, the name literally signifies "splendor of the king" or "honor of the king," emphasizing majesty and royal dignity. This etymology highlights a concept of exalted status or divine princely authority, which goes beyond a mere proper name to imply a figure associated with greatness and ruling power.
usageInScripture: The term אֲדְרַמֶּלֶךְ appears three times in Scripture, consistently referring either to an Assyrian deity or a historical figure connected to Assyria. It is translated primarily as "that Adrammelech" twice and once as "to Adrammelech," indicating its use mostly as a proper noun denoting a god worshiped by the Sepharvites or a son of Sennacherib. This consistent usage underscores its identification with foreign idolatry and Assyrian royal lineage, reflecting its dual role as both a divine name and a personal name within the biblical narrative.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding אֲדְרַמֶּלֶךְ as "honor of the king" or "splendor of the king" enriches our grasp of how pagan deities were perceived in the biblical world—figures embodying royal power and majesty but ultimately false gods. The association with Assyrian idolatry and the parricidal son of Sennacherib reveals the tragic consequences of turning away from the true God toward counterfeit sources of glory. For the Christian faith, this serves as a sober reminder that true honor and splendor belong only to the sovereign God revealed in Christ, who alone embodies perfect kingship and divine glory.
keyVerseReflection: In 2 Kings 17:31, the Sepharvites are described as burning their children in fire "to Adrammelech and Anammelech," identifying Adrammelech as one of their gods. The name here conveys not just an idol's label but the tragic reality of worship directed toward a supposed royal figure, a counterfeit king demanding extreme devotion. This underscores the grievous nature of idolatry, where the glory and honor due to God are misplaced on false gods, leading to destructive practices and spiritual ruin.
